intro.title: Welcome to Laayoune — Desert, Ocean, and Sahrawi Culture
intro.p1: Capital of the Laayoune-Sakia El Hamra region, Laayoune sits where the Sahara meets the Atlantic. The city blends a modern, airy center, a Spanish-era church, Sahrawi craftsmanship, and easy access to desert dunes and ocean beaches.
intro.p2: Most visitors spend one or two days here: start at Place du Mechouar and the artisan center, visit the Spanish church, then head to the dunes for sunset or Foum El Oued for the ocean. Khnifiss Lagoon and Tarfaya make a great day trip to the north.

mechouar.title: Place du Mechouar
mechouar.p1: Built on the occasion of King Hassan II's visit in 1985, Place du Mechouar is the civic heart of Laayoune. Its arcades open up wide vistas and make it the natural starting point for any walk through the city center.
mechouar.p2: Locals gather here in the evening: it is the ideal spot to observe daily life, sip mint tea at a nearby café, and get your bearings before heading to other sights.
mechouar.tip: Visit at sunset or early evening when the square is liveliest and the light softens the arcades.

spanish_church.title: Spanish Church (St. Francis of Assisi Cathedral)
spanish_church.p1: Located on Avenue Hassan II, the former Spanish cathedral recalls the era when Laayoune was founded under Spanish administration. Its distinctive silhouette stands out against the surrounding modern buildings.
spanish_church.p2: It is mainly admired from the outside and easily combines with a visit to nearby Place du Mechouar.
spanish_church.tip: Check locally before planning an interior visit, as visitor access can vary.

craft_center.title: Artisan Center and Markets
craft_center.p1: Near Place du Mechouar, the artisan center brings together local craftspeople and stalls offering rugs, jewelry, leather goods, and textiles inspired by Sahrawi traditions.
craft_center.p2: The surrounding markets offer a glimpse into daily local life, from fresh produce to household goods.
craft_center.tip: Compare several stalls before buying and bargain politely.

mosque.title: Laayoune Mosque and Minaret
mosque.p1: One of Laayoune's most photographed landmarks: the mosque and its minaret stand out against the desert sky, especially at sunset.
mosque.p2: Entry is reserved for Muslims, but the exterior and surrounding streets are well worth a brief stop.
mosque.tip: Dress modestly around places of worship and avoid blocking entrances during prayer times.

wadi.title: Sakia El Hamra Wadi
wadi.p1: The Sakia El Hamra wadi runs through Laayoune and gives the region its name. Its banks catch the late afternoon light, offering a peaceful contrast to the bustling center.
wadi.p2: Its water flow varies by season, meaning the landscape changes from one visit to the next.
wadi.tip: Late afternoon is the best time for a stroll and photography.

dunes.title: Laayoune Dunes (Sea of Sand)
dunes.p1: Just a few kilometers from the center along the road to Dakhla, the Laayoune dunes stretch toward the horizon: an immediate taste of the Sahara without a long journey.
dunes.p2: Sunset walks, camel rides, and 4x4 outings are the classic ways to experience them.
dunes.tip: Bring water, sunglasses, and a scarf, and avoid venturing into the dunes alone at night.

foum_el_oued.title: Foum El Oued: Beach and Corniche
foum_el_oued.p1: About 25 km west of Laayoune, Foum El Oued is the city's Atlantic gateway: a wide beach where the energy of the ocean contrasts with the silence of the desert. The renovated, well-lit corniche has become a popular evening outing for families.
foum_el_oued.p2: Buses run in the summer, while grand taxis remain the usual way to get there the rest of the year; cafés, campsites, and rental villas are available on-site.
foum_el_oued.tip: Atlantic currents can be strong: check local conditions before swimming.

el_marsa.title: El Marsa and Its Port
el_marsa.p1: El Marsa is Laayoune's port district, connected to the city by a road leading west to the ocean. Fishing boats, harbor activity, and fresh fish give it a completely different atmosphere from downtown.
el_marsa.p2: Beachfront hotels and seafood restaurants make it a convenient alternative base if you prefer sleeping by the sea.
el_marsa.tip: Ask permission before photographing fishermen or port facilities, and stay clear of working docks.

khnifiss.title: Khnifiss Lagoon (Naïla)
khnifiss.p1: North of Laayoune toward Tarfaya, Khnifiss Lagoon (Naïla) is a protected wetland where the desert meets the Atlantic, famous for its birdlife, including seasonal flamingos.
khnifiss.p2: It is best visited as a full-day 4x4 excursion or with a local guide, combined with a stop in Tarfaya.
khnifiss.tip: Hire an experienced local driver or guide and carry plenty of water and fuel.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.desc: The Place du Mechouar area is walkable; petit taxis handle city trips, grand taxis run to Foum El Oued, and a rental car or 4x4 with a driver is helpful for the dunes and Khnifiss Lagoon.

timing.title: When to Visit
timing.desc: The weather is mild from autumn to spring; favor late afternoon for the dunes and wadi, and evening for Place du Mechouar and the Foum El Oued corniche.

q1.question: How much time should I plan for Laayoune?
q1.answer: One full day allows you to see Place du Mechouar, the Spanish church, and the artisan center; add a second day for the dunes, Foum El Oued, or Khnifiss Lagoon.

q2.question: What is Laayoune best known for?
q2.answer: Laayoune is the largest city in southern Morocco's Atlantic region, known for Place du Mechouar, its nearby sand dunes, and the ocean beach of Foum El Oued.

q3.question: Can I visit Laayoune as a stopover on the southern route?
q3.answer: Yes — Laayoune is a natural stopover on the long N1 highway between Tan-Tan or Agadir and Dakhla, and it has its own airport.

q4.question: Do I need a car in Laayoune?
q4.answer: Downtown sights can be visited on foot or by petit taxi, but a car, 4x4, or driver is much more practical for the dunes, Foum El Oued, and Khnifiss Lagoon.
